title: Standard Deduction vs Itemized Deduction: Plain Words Guide
bigPicture: You get to subtract money from your income before taxes are calculated — either using one simple number (standard) or adding up your real expenses (itemized).
whatYouNeedToKnow: The standard deduction is one fixed amount the government gives you — no receipts needed.
The itemized deduction means you list out real costs like medical bills, mortgage interest, and charity donations.
You pick whichever method lowers your tax bill more — you never have to do both.
The standard deduction amount grows each year and is higher for people age 65 and older.
If your total itemized expenses are less than the standard deduction, just take the standard one.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Forgetting you get a bigger standard deduction once you turn 65.
Tossing receipts all year — if you might itemize, save every medical and donation receipt.
Assuming you must itemize because someone told you to — always compare both numbers.
Missing the state tax deduction cap of $10,000 when itemizing.
actionSteps: Gather last year's receipts for medical costs, property taxes, mortgage interest, and charity.
Add them up and compare the total to the standard deduction amount for your filing status.
Pick the bigger number and use that on your tax return.
If the numbers are close, ask a tax preparer to double-check — small differences matter.
Repeat this check every year because your expenses and the standard deduction amount can change.
